newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU wheat export award disappoints most traders.
newsitem.headline: EU wheat export award disappoints most traders.

text.p: The European Union, helped by a higher dollar, reduced wheat export subsidies on Thursday, preventing exporters from carrying out business with Egypt and Iran, according to disappointed French traders.
But EU member country officials said the Commission was satisfied with its current export pace and was eager to keep domestic prices under control after large flour sales pushed prices up.
The EU granted the export of 238,000 tonnes of soft wheat at a refund of 16.40 Ecus per tonne, nearly two Ecus below last week.
"We are very disappointed " one exporter said, adding he had expected a refund of at least 16.50 Ecus per tonne.
In France exporters had bid to export 952,500 tones of soft wheat at refunds ranging from 15.67 to 21.47 Ecus per tonne.
The latest wheat award values French wheat for March at $146 per tonne, while recent business with Iran was clinched at around $140 per tonne.
Exporters estimate that a refund of at least 18.00 Ecus is needed to cover business with Egypt or Iran.
Exporters said that one single operator grabbed most of today's licences, leaving other players in the cold.
They said that an estimated export licence short of over one million tonnes made them more vulnerable to Brussel's decisions.
Traders also said today's wheat award was a sign that the EU strategy had not changed.
They said this view was encouraged by remarks made by Guy Legras, the EU's farm director general in London on Wednesday.
Legras said he was happy with the pace of wheat exports so far and insisted he would base the value of the refund on market conditions, including the value of the dollar.
"If the dollar goes up, the refund goes down," Legras had told reporters.
"It shows the EU has gone back to its original game plan," one exporter said.
He noted that the wheat refund, helped by the higher dollar, was going back to levels seen in January and that wheat tonnage had returned to the 200,000-250,000 tonne range.
Most exporters say these tonnages are insufficient to allow the EU to export most of its crop surplus before new U.S., Canadian and Australian supplies become available in May and June.
